lines.text: A kingdom of warrior women and royal palaces, a coast scarred by the slave trade, and a nation that chose democracy. This is the story of Benin.
Around 1600 the kingdom of Dahomey rose inland from the West African coast, a tightly run state that grew rich on the trade in enslaved people.
At Abomey its kings built palace after palace, one for each reign. Their earthen walls are now a World Heritage Site.
By the early seventeen hundreds Dahomey had a regiment of women soldiers, feared in battle, whom Europeans called the Amazons.
Ghezo was born in 1790. As king for forty years, he led Dahomey at the height of its power.
Behanzin, born in 1844, would be the last independent king. When France invaded in 1892, he fought back, but could not hold them off.
Under French rule the colony kept the name Dahomey. In 1933 Mathieu Kerekou was born, the soldier who would later rule it as a Marxist state.
Nicephore Soglo, born a year later, would become the first president elected after the national conference that ended that rule.
Patrice Talon was born in 1958. The businessman would become president in 2016.
In 1960 Angelique Kidjo was born in Ouidah. Her voice would carry Benin's music around the world and win her several Grammys.
That same year Dahomey became independent from France. It took the name Benin in 1975, and became a democracy in 1991.
In December 2025 a group of soldiers tried to seize power, but the attempt failed.
From the palaces of Abomey to a democracy of its own making, Benin has come a long way.
